bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 1: Boolean retrieval
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, 2009 draft of the PDF)

question: What is information retrieval, and how do an inverted index and the Boolean retrieval model answer queries over a document collection efficiently?
contributions: Defines IR and ad hoc retrieval, precision and recall
Introduces term-document incidence matrix, inverted index, postings and sort-based index construction
Postings intersection (merge) and conjunctive query ordering by document frequency
Contrasts Boolean/extended Boolean (Westlaw) with ranked retrieval

limits: Chapter covers Boolean retrieval only: no term weighting, ranking, BM25, TF-IDF, embeddings or hybrid fusion (previewed as 'additional things we would like to be able to do', p.16).
Size figures (N=1M, 1000 words, 6 bytes, M=500K) are assumptions the authors say may vary by an order of magnitude or more, not measurements.
Westlaw figures (subscribers, 2005 default, 2007 law-librarian view) are dated to c. 2005-2007; Turtle (1994) result is given without numbers.

Dated: 'unstructured search ... conquered the world' framing predates neural and dense retrieval; web search engines are described as having only partial Boolean operators; Spotlight and Windows Vista examples are 2008-era; 'billions to trillions of words' is small by current corpora.
The claim that the inverted index is 'essentially without rivals' predates vector/ANN indexes for dense retrieval (which the chapter does not mention).
Exercise 1.13 (web engines giving non-Boolean counts for burglar AND burglar) describes 2008-9 engine behaviour and has not been rechecked.
practices: Index in advance rather than grepping at query time once collections are large, need NEAR or ranked retrieval (p.3).
Keep postings sorted by a single global docID order so lists merge in linear time (p.11).
For conjunctive queries, intersect in order of increasing document frequency, starting with the two smallest lists, using the in-memory dictionary frequencies (p.11-12).
Estimate the size of an OR by the sum of its disjuncts' frequencies when ordering general queries (p.12).
For very uneven list lengths consider binary search or hash lookup, but note these combine poorly with postings compression (p.13).
Keep the dictionary in memory and postings on disk, stored contiguously to minimise disk seeks (p.9).
Prefer variable-length arrays for rarely updated postings, linked lists when updates are frequent (p.9).
Do not rely on Boolean AND/OR to balance precision and recall; use ranked retrieval for that (p.15).

terms.definition: finding material (usually documents) of an unstructured nature (usually text) that satisfies an information need from within large collections (usually stored on computers).
Matrix element (t, d) is 1 if the play in column d contains the word in row t, and is 0 otherwise.

a model for information retrieval in which we can pose any query which is in the form of a Boolean expression of terms, that is, in which terms are combined with the operators AND, OR, and NOT. The model views each document as just a set of words.
a system aims to provide documents from within the collection that are relevant to an arbitrary user information need, communicated to the system by means of a one-off, user-initiated query.
An information need is the topic about which the user desires to know more; a query is what the user conveys to the computer in an attempt to communicate the information need.
A document is relevant if it is one that the user perceives as containing information of value with respect to their personal information need.
What fraction of the returned results are relevant to the information need?
What fraction of the relevant documents in the collection were returned by the system?

a dictionary of terms, and for each term a postings list recording which documents (and later often positions) the term occurs in; the name is redundant since an index always maps from terms back to document parts.
Each item in the list, recording that a term appeared in a document, is a posting; the list is a postings list.
the number of documents which contain each term (here also the length of each postings list)
Walk two docID-sorted postings lists with two pointers, emit equal docIDs, advance the pointer at the smaller docID.
Boolean retrieval plus additional operators such as term proximity operators.
Models such as the vector space model in which users largely use free text queries and the system decides which documents best satisfy the query.
the number of times a term occurs in a document

Algorithm for conjunctive queries that returns the set of documents containing each term in the input list of terms.

code.snippet:
INTERSECT(p1, p2)
answer <- <>
while p1 != NIL and p2 != NIL
do if docID(p1) = docID(p2)
  then ADD(answer, docID(p1)); p1 <- next(p1); p2 <- next(p2)
  else if docID(p1) < docID(p2) then p1 <- next(p1)
  else p2 <- next(p2)
return answer
